question.problem:
The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ),$ given by 

$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_______},3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ\,⟩
$$

parametrizes the hyperboloid of one sheet defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=9.$ By expressing the equation of the hyperboloid in cylindrical polar coordinates, determine the second component of $f.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that the hyperbola ${r}^{2}-{z}^{2}={k}^{2}$ can be parametrized as $⟨r,z⟩=⟨k\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,k\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩$* for $ϕ\in R.$
question.worked_solution:
If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

Substituting this into our equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-{z}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-{z}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the hyperbola ${r}^{2}-{z}^{2}=9$ represents the intersection of our hyperboloid with the plane that passes through the $z$-axis and makes the angle of $\theta $ with the positive $x$-axis. Using the hint, a parametrization of such hyperbola can be given as

$$
⟨r,z⟩=⟨3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ,\,3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩,\,ϕ\in R.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩ \\  & =⟨(3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sinh}⁡ϕ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in R.$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $3\operatorname{cosh}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
